blocks.text: My mother, Willa Woolston, who has died aged 84, was an artist, film-maker and a campaigner for survivors of child abuse.

Having experienced physical abuse in childhood herself, as an adult Willa became acutely aware that many people were living with psychological wounds from similar experiences, and planned to write a book on the subject. This vision instead became a film, My Demons (1990), in the Video Diaries series made by the BBC’s Community Programmes Unit.

Her project elicited such a strong response that Willa followed with another film, My Demons: The Legacy (1992), exploring the ripple effects of childhood abuse on families and society. The subsequent requests for help she received led Willa to establish a charity, Child Abuse Survivor Network.

Born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, she was one of the four children of Robert Woolston, a jazz drummer, and Dorothy, (nee Lohr) an artist and poet, who died four years after Willa’s birth. Robert subsequently remarried, and it was her stepmother’s treatment of Willa and her siblings that she later explored in her films.

blocks.text: After Lower Merion high school in Ardmore, Willa wanted to go to art school, but her father wished her to get a more practical qualification, and she began an education degree at Pennsylvania State University in 1960.

There she met Clair Askew, and they married in their first year, leaving education to start a family. Clair joined the US air force and in 1966 the family moved to the UK, to Felixstowe, Suffolk, where he had been stationed. After two years, Clair returned to the US, but Willa decided to stay, and she moved to London with her two children, me and my elder sister, Beth. The couple later divorced.

After a series of odd jobs, Willa went to Chelsea School of Art, graduating in the late 1970s. She combined art with her passion for jazz by drawing musicians at Soho jazz clubs such as Ronnie Scott’s or Gerry’s, resulting in exhibitions and some privately commissioned jazz portraits. She also illustrated the books B Flat, Bebop, Scat: Jazz Short Stories and Poems (1986), by Chris Parker, and The Bluesman: Musical Heritage of Black Men and Women in the Americas, by Julio Finn (1987).

After making My Demons, Willa did some more film work, including being a camera operator on Terry Jones’s Wind in the Willows (1996), but was focused on her charity, answering letters, and finding help for survivors. She also served as a director of the National Association for People Abused in Childhood.

Willa had begun living on a narrowboat on Wenlock Basin, in the eastern stretch of Regent’s Canal, in 1991, and identified strongly as a narrowboat-dweller, loving the lifestyle and staying on her boat for the rest of her life.
She is survived by me and Beth, two grandchildren, Ezekiel and Augusta, and a sister, Norma.
